Description: explicit — CJK labels in a chosen font where layers set text-font
prompt: I'm on the latest MapLibre GL JS. My style has a glyphs URL, and every label layer sets `text-font` to `["Roboto Regular"]`. Chinese place names render in the browser's default sans-serif. I want them drawn in Noto Sans SC, which I can host as a font file, without changing how the Latin labels look. How do I set that up?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
Below is a **step-by-step recipe** that lets you keep every label’s `text-font` set to  

```json
"text-font": ["Roboto Regular"]
```  

so the Latin text continues to be drawn from the glyphs server (or from the Roboto
file you already have), **but** Chinese characters will be rendered with the
Noto Sans SC font you host yourself.

The trick is to **use the style’s `font-faces` property** to attach a second font
file to the same `text-font` name, limited to the Unicode ranges that contain
CJK ideographs. When a code-point falls inside one of those ranges MapLibre will
pick the Noto Sans SC file; for everything else it falls back to the normal
Roboto glyphs (or the Roboto TTF you may also list).

---

## 1. Host the Noto Sans SC file

* Put the OTF/TTF somewhere the browser can fetch it (e.g. `https://example.com/fonts/NotoSansSC-Regular.otf`).  
* Make sure the URL is **CORS-enabled** (`Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` or your
  domain) because MapLibre loads the file through the browser.

---

## 2. Add a `font-faces` entry to the style

Edit the **root** of your style JSON (outside of `layers`, `sources`, etc.) and
add a `font-faces` object. You can keep the existing `glyphs` URL unchanged.

```json
{
  "version": 8,
  "glyphs": "https://my-glyphs.example.com/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf",
  "font-faces": {
    "Roboto Regular": [
      /* 1️⃣  The normal Roboto file – optional if you already have a glyphs URL
         for Latin.  Keeping it here makes the style work offline as well. */
      {
        "url": "https://example.com/fonts/Roboto-Regular.ttf"
      },

      /* 2️⃣  The Noto Sans SC file – only used for CJK ranges */
      {
        "url": "https://example.com/fonts/NotoSansSC-Regular.otf",
        "unicode-range": [
          "U+3000-303F",   /* CJK Symbols and Punctuation */
          "U+3040-309F",   /* Hiragana (Japanese) – optional */
          "U+30A0-30FF",   /* Katakana (Japanese) – optional */
          "U+3400-4DBF",   /* CJK Unified Ideographs Extension A */
          "U+4E00-9FFF",   /* CJK Unified Ideographs */
          "U+F900-FAFF",   /* CJK Compatibility Ideographs */
          "U+20000-2A6DF", /* CJK Unified Ideographs Extension B */
          "U+2A700-2B73F", /* CJK Unified Ideographs Extension C */
          "U+2B740-2B81F", /* CJK Unified Ideographs Extension D */
          "U+2F800-2FA1F"  /* CJK Compatibility Ideographs Supplement */
        ]
      }
    ]
  },

  /* … the rest of your style (sources, layers, etc.) … */
}
```

### Why this works

* `text-font` still resolves to the **single name** `"Roboto Regular"`.  
* When MapLibre needs a glyph it first looks at `font-faces`.  
* If the requested code-point is inside any of the `unicode-range`s of a font-face
  entry, that file is used **instead of** the glyph-PBF.  
* For all other code-points (Latin, Greek, Cyrillic, …) the first entry (or the
  glyphs server) is used, so the appearance of your existing Latin labels does
  not change.

---

## 3. (Optional) Load the `font-faces` at runtime with `map.setFontFaces()`

If you cannot edit the static style JSON (e.g. you receive the style from a
third-party server), you can inject the same object after the map is created:

```javascript
import maplibregl from 'maplibre-gl';

const map = new maplibregl.Map({
  container: 'map',
  style: 'https://my-style.example.com/style.json',
  center: [0, 0],
  zoom: 2
});

/* Wait until the style is loaded, then add the font-faces */
map.on('style.load', () => {
  map.setFontFaces({
    'Roboto Regular': [
      {
        url: 'https://example.com/fonts/Roboto-Regular.ttf'
      },
      {
        url: 'https://example.com/fonts/NotoSansSC-Regular.otf',
        'unicode-range': [
          'U+3000-303F',
          'U+3040-309F',
          'U+30A0-30FF',
          'U+3400-4DBF',
          'U+4E00-9FFF',
          'U+F900-FAFF',
          'U+20000-2A6DF',
          'U+2A700-2B73F',
          'U+2B740-2B81F',
          'U+2F800-2FA1F'
        ]
      }
    ]
  });
});
```

Calling `setFontFaces` **after** `style.load` guarantees the map has already
parsed the style’s `text-font` lists, but before any tiles are rendered.  
You can also call it **before** creating the map (e.g. in a `MapLibreGL`-compatible
framework) by passing the same object in the `fontFaces` option of the map
constructor (available from GL JS 6.7.0).

---

## 4. Verify the result

1. Open the map in a browser.  
2. Open DevTools → **Network** tab and filter by **font**. You should see a
   request for `NotoSansSC-Regular.otf` when the map first draws a Chinese
   label.  
3. Inspect a label with the inspector (`Ctrl+Shift+C`). The computed style
   should show `font-family: "Roboto Regular"` (the name you used) but the
   rendered glyphs will be the Noto Sans SC shapes.  
4. Latin labels should still look exactly as they did before (Roboto).

If you still see the browser’s generic `sans-serif`, double-check:

* The `unicode-range` strings are **exactly** as shown (no extra spaces).  
* The font file URL is reachable and CORS-enabled.  
* The `text-font` name in the layers matches the key in `font-faces` **exactly**
  (case-sensitive, spaces included).  

---

## 5. What about the `glyphs` URL?

* **Leave it** – it continues to serve the Roboto glyph PBFs for Latin, Greek,
  Cyrillic, etc.  
* The presence of `font-faces` does **not** disable the glyph server; it only
  overrides it for the ranges you declare.  

If you ever want to drop the glyph server completely (e.g. for a fully offline
app), you can add a Roboto TTF entry to `font-faces` as shown above and remove
the `glyphs` field entirely. GL JS ≥ 5.11 will then render everything locally.

---

## 6. TL;DR – Minimal change checklist

| Action | What to do |
|--------|------------|
| **Host Noto Sans SC** | Put `NotoSansSC-Regular.otf` on a CORS-enabled URL. |
| **Edit style** | Add a `font-faces` object (see JSON snippet) that maps `"Roboto Regular"` → Roboto (optional) + Noto Sans SC with the CJK `unicode-range`s. |
| **(Optional) Runtime** | Call `map.setFontFaces()` with the same object if you can’t edit the static style. |
| **Test** | Verify a Chinese label loads the `.otf` file and looks like Noto Sans SC, while Latin stays Roboto. |

That’s all you need – no changes to any `text-font` arrays, no new layers, and no
impact on the existing glyphs server for the rest of the world. Happy mapping!

**Typical hosting options**

* Put the file on the same origin that serves your style (e.g. `https://mytiles.example.com/fonts/NotoSansSC-Regular.otf`).

```json
  "version": 8,
  "glyphs": "https://mytiles.example.com/font/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf",
  "font-faces": {
    "Roboto Regular": [
      {
        "url": "https://mytiles.example.com/fonts/NotoSansSC-Regular.otf",
        "unicode-range": [
          "U+3000-30FF",   // CJK Symbols & Punctuation
          "U+3400-4DBF",   // CJK Unified Ideographs Extension A
          "U+4E00-9FFF",   // CJK Unified Ideographs
          "U+F900-FAFF",   // CJK Compatibility Ideographs
          "U+20000-2A6DF", // CJK Unified Ideographs Extension B

          "U+2B820-2CEAF", // CJK Unified Ideographs Extension E
          "U+2CEB0-2EBEF", // CJK Unified Ideographs Extension F
          "U+2F800-2FA1F", // CJK Compatibility Ideographs Supplement
          "U+FF00-FFEF"    // Half-width & Full-width Forms (includes full-width Latin)
        ]
      }
    ]
  },

    {
      "id": "place-labels",
      "type": "symbol",
      "source": "place",
      "layout": {
        "text-field": ["get", "name"],
        "text-font": ["Roboto Regular"],
        "text-size": 12
      },
      "paint": { /* … */ }
    }
    /* … other layers … */
  ]
}
```

**What this does**

* For every character **outside** the listed ranges (i.e. Latin, Greek, Cyrillic, etc.) the renderer still uses the **Roboto glyph PBFs** you already serve.  
* For any character **inside** the ranges (the Chinese characters you care about) the browser loads the **Noto Sans SC** file and draws the glyph locally via the browser’s text engine (TinySDF is bypassed for those code points).

```javascript
  center: [0, 0],
  zoom: 2,
  // keep the default; we don't need localIdeographFontFamily here
});

  map.setFontFaces({

        url: 'https://mytiles.example.com/fonts/NotoSansSC-Regular.otf',
        // same Unicode ranges as above
        'unicode-range': [
          'U+3000-30FF',
          'U+3400-4DBF',
          'U+4E00-9FFF',
          'U+F900-FAFF',
          'U+20000-2A6DF',
          'U+2A700-2B73F',
          'U+2B740-2B81F',
          'U+2B820-2CEAF',
          'U+2CEB0-2EBEF',
          'U+2F800-2FA1F',
          'U+FF00-FFEF'
        ]
      }
    ]
  });

```

> **Note** – `setFontFaces()` must be called **after** the style has loaded (`style.load` event) because the map needs the style’s `font-faces` object to exist first.

---

* The `localIdeographFontFamily` option only affects layers that **do not specify a `text-font`** (i.e. they rely on the default stack).  
* Since you *do* specify `"Roboto Regular"` on every label layer, the option is ignored for those layers.  
* **Do not set it to `false`** – that would force the map to try to fetch CJK glyph PBFs (which you don’t have) and would make the text disappear or fall back to the generic system font.

---

## 4. Verify the result

| Step | What to look for |
|------|-------------------|
| Open the map in Chrome/Firefox | Chinese place names should appear in the **Noto Sans SC** design (check the characteristic “square-ish” glyphs). |
| Open DevTools → Network → filter “font” | You should see a request for `NotoSansSC-Regular.otf` (once per page load) and **no** requests for `.../Roboto Regular/...pbf` for the same Chinese characters. |

If you prefer a cleaner separation (e.g. you might later want a different CJK font for a different style), you can add a **second name** to the `text-font` list:

```json

```

* Keep the `font-faces` entry for **both** names (Roboto for Latin, Noto for CJK).  
* The first name that has a matching glyph (or a matching `unicode-range` entry) wins, so Latin still uses Roboto, Chinese uses Noto.  

The approach shown in the answer (single name + `unicode-range`) is the most compact when you cannot edit every layer’s `text-font` list.

---

| ✅ | Action |
|---|--------|
| **Host** `NotoSansSC-Regular.otf` on a CORS-enabled URL. |
| **Add** a `font-faces` entry for **the exact same `text-font` name** (`"Roboto Regular"`). |
| **Restrict** that entry with a `unicode-range` that covers all CJK blocks you need. |
| **Leave** `glyphs` pointing at your existing Roboto PBF server (Latin continues to use it). |
| **Do not** change `localIdeographFontFamily` (default works). |
| **Test** that the network request for the OTF is made and that Chinese labels look like Noto Sans SC. |

That’s all you need—no changes to the existing Roboto glyphs, no extra layers, and no need to generate new PBFs. The browser’s text engine will handle shaping, kerning, and RTL for any script that needs it, while Latin stays crisp thanks to the pre-computed SDF glyphs. Happy mapping!

```json
          "U+3000-30FF",   // CJK Symbols & Punctuation
          "U+3400-4DBF",   // CJK Unified Ideographs Extension A
          "U+4E00-9FFF",   // CJK Unified Ideographs
          "U+F900-FAFF",   // CJK Compatibility Ideographs
          "U+20000-2A6DF", // CJK Unified Ideographs Extension B
          "U+2A700-2B73F", // CJK Unified Ideographs Extension C
          "U+2B740-2B81F", // CJK Unified Ideographs Extension D
          "U+2B820-2CEAF", // CJK Unified Ideographs Extension E
          "U+2CEB0-2EBEF", // CJK Unified Ideographs Extension F
          "U+2F800-2FA1F", // CJK Compatibility Ideographs Supplement
          "U+AC00-D7AF",   // Hangul Syllables (Korean)
          "U+1100-11FF",   // Hangul Jamo
          "U+3130-318F",   // Hangul Compatibility Jamo
          "U+FF00-FFEF"    // Half-width & Full-width Forms (includes some CJK punctuation)
        ]
      }
    ]
  },

  /* … the rest of your style (sources, layers, etc.) … */
}
```

### Why this works

* **`text-font` stays `"Roboto Regular"`** – you don’t have to touch any layer definitions.
* When MapLibre needs to draw a glyph, it first checks `font-faces`.  
  * If the code-point falls inside one of the `unicode-range` entries, the **local font file** (`NotoSansSC-Regular.otf`) is used.  
  * Otherwise it falls back to the normal glyph-PBF pipeline (your existing `glyphs` URL, which still serves Roboto for Latin, Greek, Cyrillic, etc.).
* The `unicode-range` list can be trimmed to just the blocks you actually need (e.g. only `U+4E00-9FFF` for the “basic” CJK block). Adding the extra ranges above is just a safe-guard for punctuation and Korean Hangul.

## 3. (Optional) Set the `font-faces` at runtime

If you can’t or don’t want to edit the static style JSON (e.g. you’re loading a style from a third-party service), you can inject the same mapping after the map is created:

```javascript
import maplibregl from 'maplibre-gl';

const map = new maplibregl.Map({
  container: 'map',
  style: 'https://example.com/your-style.json',
  center: [0, 0],
  zoom: 2,
  // keep the default `glyphs` URL – we’ll override only CJK locally
});

map.on('style.load', () => {
  map.setFontFaces({
    'Roboto Regular': [
      {
        url: 'https://example.com/fonts/NotoSansSC-Regular.otf',
        'unicode-range': [
          'U+3000-30FF',
          'U+3400-4DBF',
          'U+4E00-9FFF',
          'U+F900-FAFF',
          'U+20000-2A6DF',
          'U+2A700-2B73F',
          'U+2B740-2B81F',
          'U+2B820-2CEAF',
          'U+2CEB0-2EBEF',
          'U+2F800-2FA1F',
          'U+AC00-D7AF',
          'U+1100-11FF',
          'U+3130-318F',
          'U+FF00-FFEF'
        ]
      }
    ]
  });
});
```

`map.setFontFaces()` does exactly the same thing as the static `font-faces` property, but lets you compute URLs or ranges dynamically.

## 4. Verify the result

1. Open the map in a browser.
2. Open DevTools → **Network** tab and filter by **font** or **pbf**.
   * You should see **no** `*.pbf` requests for any CJK code-points (the glyph server is bypassed).
   * You should see a single **GET** request for `NotoSansSC-Regular.otf` (or the cached version if you reload).
3. Inspect a Chinese label with the **Elements** panel → **Computed → font-family**. It should list the URL-loaded Noto font (or at least show `Noto Sans SC` as the first family).

If you still see the browser’s generic `sans-serif`, double-check:

* The `unicode-range` strings are **exactly** as shown (no extra spaces, proper `U+` prefix).
* The font file is reachable and served with correct CORS headers.
* The `text-font` name in the style matches the key in `font-faces` **character-for-character** (`"Roboto Regular"` – case-sensitive, spaces included).

---

## 5. What about `localIdeographFontFamily`?

`localIdeographFontFamily` only applies when a layer **does not** specify a `text-font` (i.e. it uses the default `"sans-serif"` stack). Because your layers *do* set `"Roboto Regular"`, that option is ignored. The `font-faces` approach above is the recommended way to override CJK rendering while keeping the existing `text-font` value.

| ✅ | Action |

| **Host** `NotoSansSC-Regular.otf` with CORS. |
| **Add** a `font-faces` entry for `"Roboto Regular"` that points to the Noto file and limits it to the CJK Unicode ranges you need. |
| **Leave** `glyphs` unchanged – it will continue to serve Roboto for Latin, Greek, Cyrillic, etc. |
